source.title: FDA Approves First Oral PCSK9 Inhibitor to Lower LDL Cholesterol in Adults with High Cholesterol

sentences.sentence: The US FDA approved Lipfendra (enlicitide) on 17 July 2026, the first oral medicine that inhibits PCSK9, to lower LDL cholesterol in adults.
The US FDA approved Lipfendra (enlicitide) on 17 July 2026 and calls it the first oral therapy to inhibit PCSK9.
It is an add-on to diet and exercise for adults with high cholesterol, including those with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia.
The FDA says the approval rests on two trials that compared LDL cholesterol with placebo after 24 weeks.
This is a US decision; UK availability is decided separately.
On 17 July 2026 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Lipfendra (enlicitide), which it describes as the first oral therapy that inhibits PCSK9.
It is approved as an add-on to diet and exercise to lower LDL cholesterol in adults with high cholesterol, including adults with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia.
LDL cholesterol is the type often called bad cholesterol.
The medicine is a tablet taken by mouth.
The FDA notes that several kinds of medicine already lower LDL cholesterol, including statins, ezetimibe and injectable PCSK9 inhibitors.
It says the approval rests on two trials in which the main measure was the change in LDL cholesterol from the start to week 24, compared with placebo.
One trial enrolled adults with, or at high risk of, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and the other enrolled only adults with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia.
In the first trial the FDA reports that adverse reactions occurred about as often with Lipfendra as with placebo.
This is a US decision; availability in the UK is decided separately by the MHRA and NICE.

source.title: FDA Approves New Treatment to Reduce Proteinuria in Adults with Primary Immunoglobulin A Nephropathy

sentences.sentence: The US FDA granted accelerated approval to Trutakna (atacicept-vymj) on 7 July 2026 to reduce protein in the urine in adults with primary IgA nephropathy.
The US FDA granted accelerated approval to Trutakna (atacicept-vymj) on 7 July 2026.
It is an injection for adults with primary IgA nephropathy at risk of disease progression.
The approval rests on a reduction in proteinuria; the FDA says it is not established whether the medicine slows kidney function decline.
This is a US decision; UK availability is decided separately.
On 7 July 2026 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted accelerated approval to Trutakna (atacicept-vymj), an injection given under the skin.
It is approved for adults with primary IgA nephropathy, a kidney disease, who are at risk of the disease getting worse.
The FDA describes it as the first approved medicine that targets both BAFF and APRIL, two signalling proteins involved in the survival and maturation of certain immune cells.
Accelerated approval here rests on a reduction in proteinuria, which means protein in the urine.
The FDA states that it has not been established whether Trutakna slows the decline in kidney function over the long term, and that an ongoing trial must be completed to confirm this.
The efficacy and safety data come from a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in adults with biopsy-confirmed IgA nephropathy.
This is a US decision; availability in the UK is decided separately by the MHRA and NICE.

source.title: FDA Approves First-of-Its-Kind Chronic Hepatitis B Treatment

sentences.sentence: The US FDA approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) on 20 October 2026, the first antisense oligonucleotide approved for chronic hepatitis B in certain adults.
The US FDA approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) on 20 October 2026.
The FDA calls it the first antisense oligonucleotide approved to treat chronic hepatitis B.
It is for certain adults without cirrhosis and is used alongside existing antiviral therapy.
This is a US decision; UK availability is decided separately.
On 20 October 2026 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) for chronic hepatitis B.
The FDA says it is the first approved antisense oligonucleotide for chronic hepatitis B.
It is approved for certain adults without cirrhosis, as an addition to existing antiviral therapy.

The FDA says eligible patients have taken antiviral therapy for at least six months, have suppressed virus levels, and have a hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) level below a set threshold measured with an FDA-authorised test.
The FDA reports that 24 weeks after stopping all hepatitis B treatment, 19% of the patients who had received Hibsago still had the virus under control.
The FDA granted the medicine Fast Track and Breakthrough Therapy designations, and its application received Priority Review.
This is a US decision; availability in the UK is decided separately by the MHRA and NICE.
